about: The onboarding v2 questions (spec smf-spec-onboarding-v2.md rev 11, 'The questions', and rev 12 'Next phase'), shared by both page designs: A, one long page (--layout one-page), and B, one question at a time (--layout steps). The 31 core fields are numbered 1-31 and progress counts them and nothing else; Go deeper is optional and never counted. Each field says where its answer is stored in the answers file (intake.schema.json): 'key' is the answer, 'path' a part inside a group answer (positioning, teach, deep), and each part names the property it fills. Examples describe what the made-up bakery said; they never pre-fill a box and never suggest this brand's beliefs, stories or proof. Fields marked never_draft (F8 B, D, E) only ever hold the person's own words. 'extra' holds rev 12's optional, uncounted questions, each shown right after the field named in 'after'.
about_five_steps: Spec rev 14 (design review, Oct 22): onboarding is five steps, then 'one more thing' (rules); every other question is in 'Make it better', reachable any time and never in the main route. Each question keeps its own Confirm.
about_needed: Oct 23 (Joe, plain-reader audit): the five answers a first post needs are marked 'Needed to write your first post'; every other question says 'Optional'. Skipping stays possible; the finish screen says what's still needed.

needed_names.name: your brand name
needed_names.voice_samples: a few things you've written or said

deep_groups.title: What you stand for, the rest

core.ask: What's your brand called, exactly as people say it?
core.why: It goes on every post and picture, so the spelling has to be perfect.
core.example: The bakery wrote its name the way it's on the shop sign: “Maple & Main Bakery”.

core.ask: Which website or handle (your @name) should appear on your pictures?
core.why: It's printed on every carousel and card, so people can find you.
core.example: The bakery chose its website, example.com.

core.ask: What do you do, and for whom?
core.hint: Include how you help them, drawing on your own experience.
core.why: Everything the Social Media Factory writes starts from this.
core.example: A neighbourhood sourdough bakery; bread every morning, and weekend classes for home bakers who keep getting flat loaves.

core.ask: Who are you trying to reach?
core.why: Posts land when they're written for one clear person.
core.example: People nearby who care about good bread, and home bakers anywhere who want to understand sourdough.

parts.name: in_the_way
parts.label: What's in their way (one per line)

core.ask: What's in their way?
core.why: The problems your audience has are the best topics you'll ever have.
core.example: Their loaves come out dense; they think they need special equipment.

core.ask: What questions do they really ask you?
core.why: Real questions, in their words, make posts people stop for.
core.example: “Why is my sourdough dense?” “Can I bake good bread in a normal oven?”

core.ask: What objections do you hear, and how do you answer them?
core.why: Answering doubts before people raise them is how posts turn into customers.
core.example: “A class is too expensive.” The bakery answers: you leave with a starter and a method you'll use for years.

core.ask: Who speaks in your posts: you, the company, or both?
core.why: Names and handles must be spelled exactly, so each one needs your tap.
core.example: A person (the head baker, by name, with her role) and the company account.

core.ask: Why did you start, in a few sentences?
core.why: Your origin is the story people remember and repeat.
core.example: Every bakery on the high street sold the same frozen loaf, so the owner started baking the slow way.

core.ask: Paste or type a few things you've really written or said.
core.why: Your own words teach it how you sound. They're saved word for word, never tidied.
core.example: A short video you've made (paste what you said), posts, an email to a customer, or a transcript of you talking. No posts yet? Just talk for a minute.

parts.name: register
parts.label: How you sound, in a sentence or two

core.ask: How do you sound? What do you always do, and never do?
core.why: This keeps every post sounding like you, not like a robot.
core.example: Warm, plain and specific. Always give the number; never call anything “artisanal”.

parts.name: signature_phrases
parts.label: Phrases you're known for (one per line)

core.ask: Any signature phrases you're known for?
core.why: Signature phrases make you recognisable. (Words you never use are with the rules.)
core.example: “Time is an ingredient.” Never: “artisanal”, “mouthwatering”.

parts.name: value
parts.label: What they should think of first

core.ask: When someone hears your name, what should they think of first?
core.why: One clear idea is what makes a brand stick.
core.example: The bakery said: “the bakery that takes two days”.

core.ask: What do you believe about your industry that most in it don't?
core.why: A belief worth arguing about is what makes people follow you, not just like a post.
core.example: The bakery said: “Bread should take two days, not two hours.” “None” is a fine answer.

core.ask: Name two things you want to be known for, and two you're against.
core.why: Standing for and against something gives your content a point of view.
core.example: The bakery is for slow bread; against “fresh-baked” from frozen dough.

core.ask: What do others in your space do or say that you disagree with, and what do you do instead?
core.why: The contrast between you and everyone else is what people remember.
core.example: Others bake from frozen at 5am; the bakery starts the dough two days ahead.

core.ask: What three to five things must every piece of your content show, no matter what?
core.why: These become the checklist every post is held to.
core.example: The bakery: show real hands and real ovens; never call frozen “fresh”.

core.ask: Your story in three parts: what you saw that others didn't, what you believe, how you've proved it.
core.why: This is the spine of your brand: every post can point back to it.
core.example: Saw: every bakery sold the same frozen loaf. Believes: time is the ingredient nobody can fake. Proved: two-day dough, every loaf, since opening day.

core.ask: Where are you most at home, and roughly how big is your audience?
core.why: It decides which formats to lean on, and what advice fits where you are now.
core.example: The bakery is most at home on short video, with an audience under 100,000.

core.ask: What myths does your audience believe?
core.why: Busting a myth is one of the most shared kinds of post.
core.example: “Sourdough has to taste sour.”

core.ask: What mistakes do they make?
core.why: Naming a mistake shows you know their world from the inside.
core.example: “Rushing the prove.”

core.ask: What are the steps to the result you help them get?
core.why: Steps turn into carousels and how-to posts almost by themselves.
core.example: Feed the starter at the same time each day; mix the dough the evening before; bake hot, with steam.

core.ask: Your free gift: what do people get for free?
core.why: A free first step is how strangers turn into customers.
core.example: A starter feeding card. “None yet” is fine.

core.ask: Your entry offer: the smallest thing people can buy.
core.why: A small first purchase builds trust for the bigger ones.
core.example: A weekly bread subscription. “None yet” is fine.

core.ask: Your main offer: what most of your business comes from.
core.why: Most of your posts should lead here, one way or another.
core.example: A Saturday sourdough class. “None yet” is fine.

core.ask: Your premium offer: the biggest thing you sell.
core.why: Fewer people buy it, but it shapes how people see you.
core.example: A private bake day for a team. “None yet” is fine.

core.ask: Any rules your posts must follow?
core.why: Rules keep you out of trouble. They need your tap, because they're never guessed.
core.example: A bakery has no regulator, but it might never name its suppliers and always have the owner sign off.

core.ask: Your background, your main text, and the one colour people remember you by.
core.why: Your pictures come out in your colours from the very first one.
core.example: A warm cream background, a dark brown text and a burnt orange accent.

core.ask: What do you want to make, and where will you post?
core.why: So your posts are the kinds you want, made for the places you post.
core.example: The bakery wants to be the trusted name; the head baker posts on Instagram and TikTok; most people find it walking past or by word of mouth.

parts.name: hours_per_week
parts.label: Hours a week you can give it

parts.name: posts_per_week
parts.label: Posts a week that feel realistic

core.ask: How much can you keep up each week?
core.why: A plan you can keep beats a perfect plan you drop in week two.
core.example: Three hours a week, one weekend helper, four posts.

core.ask: What can you show: real work, results or examples people can see?
core.why: Showing beats telling. This is your shortlist; nothing here is ever published without your OK.
core.example: Photos of the morning bake; a class where every student left with a loaf.

extra.ask: Who will speak in your videos, and where would you film?
extra.why: Short video is where most people find you, so it helps to know who's on camera and where.
extra.example: The head baker talks to camera in the shop at 6am; the company account uses a voice-over on bake-day clips.

extra.ask: How do people find you today?
extra.why: Knowing what already works (word of mouth, Google, a market stall) helps us build on it.
extra.example: Word of mouth from regulars; the Saturday farmers market; Google Maps.

extra.ask: Who inspires you, or whose content do you love?
extra.why: We learn how they open, pace and lay out a piece. We never copy their words.
extra.example: Chad Robertson, for how he shows a whole bake in one short video.

parts.name: value
parts.label: What they'd do instead (one per line)

deep.ask: If you didn't exist, what would your customers do instead?
deep.why: It shows who you're really up against.

parts.name: known_for
parts.label: What you must be known for

deep.ask: Work back from the end: what do you want to happen, and what does that take?
deep.why: It connects today's posts to where you're going.

deep.ask: What do people compliment you on that you could lean into?
deep.why: What others already notice is often your strongest angle.

parts.name: repeatable
parts.label: Two formats you could repeat 50 times (one per line)

deep.ask: Which formats could you make again and again?
deep.why: Repeatable formats are how you keep going without burning out.

deep.ask: What topics next to your core serve the same buyer?
deep.why: Neighbouring topics keep content fresh without losing your audience.

parts.name: people
parts.label: People who keep coming up (one per line)

deep.ask: Your brand world: the people, places and interests in your stories.
deep.why: A recognisable world makes people feel they know you.

parts.name: values
parts.label: Your values and where they come from (one per line)

parts.name: never_compromise
parts.label: What you'd never compromise on (one per line)

parts.name: early_signs
parts.label: Early signs it's working (one per line)

parts.name: ambitions
parts.label: Where you want to be in three to five years

deep.why: The more the Social Media Factory knows you, the more it sounds like you.

deep.ask: Your origin story: why you started.
deep.why: Skip any you don't have; nothing is ever invented.
People trust honesty about what went wrong more than success.

deep.ask: A success story: before and after.

deep.why: Only share what you're allowed to.

deep.ask: An industry insight: a trend, mistake or shift you've seen.
deep.why: Skip it if nothing comes to mind.

parts.name: hangouts
parts.label: Where they spend time (one per line)

parts.name: trust_triggers
parts.label: What would make them trust you (one per line)

deep.why: It decides where and how to reach them.

parts.name: customer_journey
parts.label: How someone goes from stranger to customer

parts.name: dream_result
parts.label: The dream result you help them get

parts.name: dm_tool
parts.label: The tool you use for direct messages, if any

deep.why: It helps posts lead people to the right next step.

parts.name: analogies
parts.label: Comparisons you like to use (one per line)

parts.name: examples
parts.label: Examples you approve of: a bio, a post, an email (one per line)

deep.why: Approved examples are the clearest guide to how you sound.

item_parts.name: value
item_parts.label: A name, phrase or word you use your own way

deep.ask: Your own words for your ideas.
deep.why: Named ideas are used exactly as you say them.

deep.ask: If your audience only saw one piece of your content a week, what would you want it to be?
deep.why: A podcast, a long video, a newsletter: “None yet” is a fine answer.

parts.name: extra_colors
parts.label: More colours, as hex codes (one per line)

deep.why: It helps every picture feel like yours.

deep.ask: Your proof, one piece at a time.
deep.why: Real results, told in six short parts, are what make people trust you. No big wins yet? Choose “Something I'm learning or testing” instead: it's recorded honestly, never passed off as a result. Nothing here is published unless you say so.
